The SGD update θ_{j+1} = θ_j − η_j Σ_{i∈B_j} ∇ℓ(θ_j, z_i) makes θ_j − θ_{j+1} = η_j Σ_{i∈B_j} ∇ℓ(θ_j, z_i), so ∇f(θ_j)·(θ_j − θ_{j+1}) = η_j Σ_{i∈B_j} ∇f(θ_j)·∇ℓ(θ_j, z_i) by linearity of the inner product. Accumulating over all steps j containing z_i yields the standard TracIn score. No mathematical error.

results.content:
f^{return}(θ) := E_{τ ∼ π^{ref}, (s,a) ∼ τ} [ log π_θ(a | s) · (−\hat{A}^{ref}(s, a)) ].

Maximizing f^{return}(θ) encourages increasing the probability of better-than-average actions and decreasing worse-than-average ones, capturing the essence of improving expected return while being tractable.
results.route_rationale: Non-trivial sign/behaviour claim about a core target function: 'maximizing f^return encourages increasing better-action probability'. Formalized by instantiating the paper's own definitions in a two-action example and machine-checking the monotonicity of the resulting objective.

lean_result.reasoning: Formalised the paper's characterization of f^return in a faithful two-action instantiation of its own definitions: single state s, actions a1/a2, reference policy π^ref uniform (probability 1/2 each), advantages Â(s,a1)=+1 (better-than-average), Â(s,a2)=−1 (worse-than-average), and current policy π_θ(a1|s)=q, π_θ(a2|s)=1−q. The definition f^return(θ) = E[log π_θ(a|s)·(−Â^ref(s,a))] then reduces to f(q) = (log(1−q) − log q)/2. The paper's claim entails that f is monotone increasing in q on (0,1) (raising the probability of the better-than-average action should raise the objective). Lean 4 proves the negation, theorem paper_claim_false : ¬ MonotoneOn (fun q : ℝ => (Real.log (1 - q) - Real.log q) / 2) (Set.Ioo 0 1), which compiles cleanly (exit 0, axioms propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound, no sorry). Concretely f(1/4) = (log 3)/2 > 0 = f(1/2) with 1/4 < 1/2, so f is not increasing; in fact f is strictly decreasing on (0,1) since f'(q) = −(1/(1−q) + 1/q)/2 < 0. Hence maximizing f^return drives q → 0: it decreases the probability of the better-than-average action, contradicting the paper. This is a sign error in the definition (or in the stated maximization behaviour).

lean.formal_statement:
def fReturn (q : ℝ) : ℝ := (Real.log (1 - q) - Real.log q) / 2

theorem paper_claim_false : ¬ MonotoneOn fReturn (Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1) := by
  intro hmono
  have hlt : (1 / 4 : ℝ) < 1 / 2 := by norm_num
  have hmem1 : (1 / 4 : ℝ) ∈ Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1 := by norm_num
  have hmem2 : (1 / 2 : ℝ) ∈ Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1 := by norm_num
  have hle : fReturn (1 / 4 : ℝ) ≤ fReturn (1 / 2 : ℝ) := hmono hmem1 hmem2 (le_of_lt hlt)
  rw [fReturn_half] at hle
  have hpos : 0 < fReturn (1 / 4 : ℝ) := fReturn_quarter_pos
  linarith

findings.evidence: The definition $f^{\text{return}}(\theta) := \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi^{\text{ref}}, (s,a) \sim \tau}[\log \pi_\theta(a|s) \cdot (-\hat{A}^{\text{ref}}(s,a))]$ carries a minus sign on the advantage, yet the paper claims 'Maximizing $f^{\text{return}}(\theta)$ encourages increasing the probability of better-than-average actions'. In a faithful two-action instantiation of the paper's definitions (single state $s$, actions $a_1,a_2$, $\pi^{\text{ref}}$ uniform, $\hat{A}(s,a_1)=+1$, $\hat{A}(s,a_2)=-1$, $\pi_\theta(a_1|s)=q$, $\pi_\theta(a_2|s)=1-q$) the objective is $f(q) = (\log(1-q) - \log q)/2$. Lean 4 formally refutes that this is increasing on $(0,1)$ (theorem `paper_claim_false : ¬ MonotoneOn fReturn (Set.Ioo 0 1)` compiles clean); it is strictly decreasing there since $f'(q) = -(1/(1-q) + 1/q)/2 < 0$, so maximizing $f^{\text{return}}$ drives $q \to 0$ — the probability of the better-than-average action goes *down*, the opposite of the paper's claim. The consistent reading is a sign error: $f^{\text{return}}$ should use $+\hat{A}^{\text{ref}}$ (as the RLHF variant $f^{\text{seq}}$ in §5.3 does), or the characterization should say minimizing. The sign of every $f^{\text{return}}$-based influence score $I_i$ is inverted relative to the stated intent.

summary: Verified the mathematics of 'A Snapshot of Influence: A Local Data Attribution Framework for Online Reinforcement Learning' (NeurIPS 2025). Eleven self-contained equations were extracted and routed: 10 to informal review (`verify-math`) and 1 to formal Lean 4 verification (`verify-math-lean`) against the shared project `MATH_VERIFICATION/Paper` (reused from a prior run; kept on disk, `lean_project_kept=true`). The single Lean-routed snippet — the return target function $f^{\text{return}}$ together with the claim that 'maximizing $f^{\text{return}}$ encourages increasing the probability of better-than-average actions' — was formally **REFUTED**: in a faithful two-action instantiation of the paper's own definitions the objective $(\log(1-q) - \log q)/2$ is strictly decreasing, not increasing, so maximizing it drives the probability of the better-than-average action to zero. This is a sign error in the definition (or in the stated maximization behaviour); the RLHF variant $f^{\text{seq}}$ in §5.3 uses $+\hat{A}^{\text{ref}}$ with no minus sign, corroborating that the minus in $f^{\text{return}}$ is the anomaly. Severity is rated *minor*: the framework and the empirical claims (IIF improves training) survive a sign correction, and relative filtering is sign-agnostic. All 10 other snippets — TracIn derivation, PPO clipped surrogate, $f^{\text{action}}$, the influence formula $I_i$, graph roughness, the sample-efficiency metric, $f^{\text{seq}}$, the MC advantage identity, TD error, and the PER priority weights — were checked informally and contain no critical mathematical errors. One notational slip was noted in §3.1: the $I_i$ formula evaluates the target gradient at $\theta_0^{(k)}$ while the surrounding prose says $\theta_j^{(k)}$; §5.1 clarifies the intended design (use only $\theta^{(k)}$), so this is documentation, not mathematics. No Lean `FAILED` occurred, so no informal fallbacks were run. Verdict: **MINOR_ERRORS**.
